title: Ordering food
description: Order a meal, and say what you want with it.
grammar: con and sin, and the article in an order
grammarNote: Con is with and sin is without: un café con leche, un café sin azúcar.

explanation.summary: Ordering is simple once you know two small words: con, with, and sin, without. Everything else is the vocabulary of a café, and the rule that an order takes un or una.

sections.heading: Con and sin
sections.body: Con is with and sin is without. Both go straight after the thing they modify: un café con leche, un café sin azúcar. They are used for what comes with a dish or a drink, not for people: con mi hermana means with my sister.

examples.es: Un café con leche, por favor.

sections.heading: What you order takes an article
sections.body: In an order the noun takes un or una, never el: quiero un café, quiero una tortilla. The article says you mean one of them, which is exactly what an order is.

examples.es: Para mí, una sopa de verduras.

sections.heading: Asking what there is
sections.body: ¿Qué hay? asks what there is. A waiter answers con una tortilla de patatas y una ensalada. The word for the bill, which you already know, is la cuenta.

examples.es: Hay sopa de verduras y pescado.
examples.en: There is vegetable soup and fish.

items.note: Masculine: el menú. The accent marks the stress.
Masculine: el camarero. The feminine is la camarera.
Masculine: el plato. It also means a plate.
Masculine: el vaso. It also means a drinking glass.
An infinitive ending in -ar: encargo, encargas, encarga.

drills.note: An order takes un or una.
Con goes straight after the thing it modifies.
